passage: I was nine when I asked if God is real. At home, Nani said, "Of course, God sees everything, beta." Next morning at school I asked Sarika Ma'am. She did not say yes or no. She said, "People believe different things. Some believe in God, some don't, and many are still wondering. What do you think?" I said I didn't know. She said that was an honest answer. That night I told Nani, "Ma'am says people believe different things." Nani was quiet, then said, "That is true too. In our family we pray." I thought about it for days. It was strange to have two answers, but nobody was angry. I still ask questions, and no one tells me I'm wrong for asking. Parveen

qa.q: What did Sarika Ma'am say when Parveen asked if God is real?
qa.a: Sarika Ma'am said that people believe different things, that some believe in God, some don't, and many are still wondering, and asked what Parveen thought.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel about getting two different answers?
qa.a: Parveen felt curious and calm. It was strange to have two answers, but nobody was angry, so Parveen kept thinking about it.

qa.q: Which choice by Nani kept trust between her and Parveen?
qa.a: Nani stayed quiet, then said that what Ma'am said is true too and that in their family they pray, instead of arguing.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt when Parveen repeated what Ma'am said?
qa.a: Probably thoughtful and a little surprised, since she went quiet first, but she was willing to accept it.

grounding: A child asks whether God is real and gets different answers at home and at school, and calm honest replies that people believe differently keep curiosity and trust.

passage: Note to Jaya's parents, Class 5. During circle time today, Jaya, eight, asked, "Does God really exist? My Nani says yes, but my friend's father says no." The class went quiet. I said, "People believe different things, and that is allowed. Some people pray, some don't. What do you think, Jaya?" Jaya said, "I think maybe yes, but I want to find out." I told her that asking is good, and that she can talk with her family about what they believe. Two other children shared what their families believe, and nobody laughed. Jaya seemed relaxed afterwards. I would gently encourage you to keep answering her questions calmly. Vasudha, class teacher

qa.q: What did Jaya ask during circle time?
qa.a: Jaya asked, "Does God really exist?" and said Nani says yes but a friend's father says no.

qa.q: What might Jaya be feeling when she says "I think maybe yes, but I want to find out"?
qa.a: Jaya is curious and thoughtful, and feels safe enough to say she is unsure and wants to explore.

qa.q: Which choice by Vasudha kept the class calm and curious?
qa.a: Vasudha said that people believe different things and that this is allowed, and asked Jaya what she thinks instead of giving one answer.

qa.q: How might the two other children have felt when they shared their family beliefs?
qa.a: Probably safe and included, since nobody laughed and the teacher said that different beliefs are allowed.

grounding: A child asks whether God is real and the teacher answers calmly that people believe differently, protecting the child's curiosity and trust.

passage:
When I was nine, I asked my Ammi, "Is Allah real?" She said, "Of course, Hafsa. He made everything." Then at school, my best friend Irawati said her family doesn't believe in any God. "Papa says people made up gods to feel safe."
I didn't know who to believe. I got scared that one of them was lying. At night I couldn't sleep.
So I asked our class teacher. She put down her pen and said, "That's a big question, Hafsa. People believe different things. Your Ammi believes in Allah. Irawati's family doesn't believe in God. You can love both of them and keep thinking."
Then I asked Ammi again. She was quiet, then said, "Irawati's family are good people too. Keep asking questions."
I still ask questions. Irawati is still my best friend.

qa.q: What did Irawati's Papa say about gods?
qa.a: Papa says people made up gods to feel safe.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa have trouble sleeping?
qa.a: Hafsa felt confused and scared, worrying that either Ammi or Irawati was lying.

qa.q: What made the teacher's answer helpful?
qa.a: The teacher stayed calm and explained that people believe different things, so Hafsa could keep loving both and keep thinking.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel if Hafsa had been told her family was wrong?
qa.a: Irawati might feel hurt and left out, and the friendship could have suffered.

grounding: A child asks whether God is real, gets different answers at home and from a friend, and calm replies that people believe differently protect the child's curiosity and trust.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 3, Friday.
During story time today, Darshan, eight, suddenly asked, "Ma'am, is God real?" Sudha answered before I could: "My papa says no." Darshan looked shocked. "My Dadi says yes! She prays every morning!" Two children laughed. Darshan went quiet and pulled at his sleeve.
I sat down on the mat with them. I said, "That's a very good question. Some families believe in God, some believe in many, some don't believe. People believe differently, and all of them can be kind. You can ask your family what they think."
Darshan asked, "So nobody's wrong?" I said, "Everybody can keep asking."
Next step: I will send a short note home to both families so they know what came up and how I answered it.

qa.q: What did Sudha say her papa says?
qa.a: Sudha said, "My papa says no."

qa.q: What does Darshan pulling at his sleeve suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt confused and embarrassed after hearing a different answer and seeing two children laugh.

qa.q: Why was the teacher's reply a good one?
qa.a: The teacher stayed calm, said people believe differently and can all be kind, and invited the children to keep asking, which protected curiosity and trust.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel after the teacher's answer?
qa.a: Sudha might feel relieved that her family's view wasn't called wrong, and that she wasn't in trouble for saying it.

grounding: A teacher's note shows children with different home answers about God, and a calm reply that people believe differently protects curiosity and trust.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today in moral science Sir said God is watching everything. At home, Papa says he isn't sure if God exists at all. Mumma prays every night. So who is right?
I asked Papa at dinner. He didn't laugh. He said, "Seema, I don't know for sure. Mumma believes, and I respect that. Some people believe, some don't, and some keep wondering, like me."
Mumma said, "And you can decide for yourself when you're older. You can ask me anything."
Chaitanya, my little brother, said, "I think God is a big cat." Everyone laughed, even Papa.
I felt better. I thought it was bad that my parents think different things, but it isn't. They still hold hands on the balcony.
I will keep wondering. That's allowed.
Seema

qa.q: What did Chaitanya say he thinks God is?
qa.a: Chaitanya said, "I think God is a big cat."

qa.q: How did Seema feel after talking with her parents?
qa.a: Seema felt relieved and calmer, realising it wasn't bad that Seema's parents think different things.

qa.q: What did Papa and Mumma do that protected Seema's trust?
qa.a: They answered honestly and calmly, each respecting the other's view, and told Seema she could keep asking and decide for herself.

qa.q: How might Seema's teacher's words look different after the family talk?
qa.a: Seema may now see the teacher's words as one belief among many, rather than a fact that makes her father wrong.

grounding: A child hears different answers about God at school and home, and the parents' honest, calm replies protect the child's curiosity and trust.

passage: In the town school at Hosur, Sudha raised her hand during the lesson on the moon. "Ma'am, is God real?" A few children gasped. Ayesha whispered, "Of course. Allah is real." Ramesh said his grandfather didn't believe in any god. Mrs. Nair put the chalk down. "People believe very differently, Sudha. Many people in this room believe in God, in different ways. Some people don't. It's a big question, and you can keep asking it." At home that evening Sudha asked Paati, who was lighting the lamp. Paati said, "God is real to me, kanna. When you're older you'll think about it yourself." Sudha lay on the mat, looking at the ceiling fan, turning both answers over like two smooth stones.

qa.q: Who was lighting the lamp when Sudha asked at home?
qa.a: Paati was lighting the lamp.

qa.q: What might Sudha be feeling as she lies on the mat turning both answers over?
qa.a: Sudha seems curious and thoughtful rather than scared, calmly comparing the two answers.

qa.q: How did Mrs. Nair's reply protect Sudha's curiosity?
qa.a: She answered calmly and honestly that people believe differently, did not scold the question, and said Sudha could keep asking.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt when the teacher said some people don't believe in God?
qa.a: Ayesha, sure that Allah is real, might have felt surprised or unsettled, but the calm answer also respected Ayesha's own belief.

grounding: It illustrates a child asking whether God is real and getting different but calm, honest answers at school and at home that keep curiosity and trust safe.
